By contrast, reporting remains heterogeneous, as illustrated by the variability among national dashboards documented in the section on real-world implementation.

Two assessments by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine have outlined the characteristics required for a mature wastewater surveillance system. The first envisages a national wastewater surveillance system that is flexible, equitable, sustainable, integrated, and actionable. Flexibility refers to the capacity to monitor multiple pathogens simultaneously and adapt rapidly to emerging threats; equity concerns representation and coverage across population groups, including efforts to extend surveillance capacity to communities without sewer connections; and integration refers to triangulation with other disease surveillance systems [120]. The second focuses on translating such a system into public-health action and gives particular attention to how wastewater data are shared, interpreted, and presented [108]. Together, these reports emphasize that mature WBS depends on system design, data integration, and reporting infrastructure in addition to analytical methods. This is consistent with the discussion in the section on methodological complexities, where transferability depends on cross-site differences in data generation and surveillance context.

Interoperable data structures provide a concrete area for analytical standardization. The PHES-ODM data model introduced in the section on data harmonization and normalization provides an early implementation, specifying how sites, samples, measurements, methods, and contextual metadata are represented to support more consistent combination of datasets across programmes [80]. An equivalent convention for analytical reporting, however, has not yet been established: no widely adopted standard exists for reporting the model family or analytical approach used, the validation design, the treatment of censored measurements, or the baseline against which performance was assessed. As discussed in the section on methodological complexities, these details are often reported in insufficient depth to support clear interpretation of published results. Extending harmonization from measurement to analytical reporting would improve the comparability and interpretation of published models.

Such interoperability and reporting frameworks should be co-designed by data scientists, microbiologists, engineers, wastewater utilities, epidemiologists, and public-health agencies. The interdisciplinary coordination barriers described in the section on real-world implementation indicate that their development will require deliberate cross-disciplinary coordination, including shared forums, agreements, and translation between technical and public-health domains.

sections.title: Multimodal data fusion and integrated surveillance

paragraphs.en: Multimodal fusion can occur both analytically, through the integration of heterogeneous data streams, and operationally, through complementary sampling that broadens population and infrastructure coverage.

sections.title: Integration of epidemiological, mobility, and sequencing data

paragraphs.en: Multimodal fusion can integrate wastewater signals with the epidemiological and contextual data needed for their interpretation. Potential inputs include wastewater measurements, clinical and syndromic indicators, anonymized mobility data, environmental and operational variables, and amplicon or metagenomic sequencing data from both wastewater and clinical samples [60,120,121]. Existing studies show that combining selected data streams can add information. Schenk et al. compared four SARIMAX specifications for predicting SARS-CoV-2 cases in Liechtenstein and two Austrian regions – active cases alone, active cases with wastewater data, active cases with mobility data, and a combined model incorporating restriction policies – and found that adding mobility data and restriction information improved predictive precision beyond what wastewater measurements alone provided [57]. At the spatial scale, Tierney et al. integrated targeted amplicon and bulk metatranscriptomic sequencing across 2,238 samples from geospatially distinct areas of Miami-Dade County, tracked SARS-CoV-2 variants with close correspondence to PCR results from university students and hospital patients, and showed that bacterial content at sampling points serving small populations carried information on host-derived microorganisms associated with human health and diet [69]. Future spatio-temporal models could integrate pathogen circulation, human behaviour, environmental conditions, and local infrastructure, while being evaluated for interpretability and external validity under the designs set out in the section on methodological complexities [61,69]. Where data-sharing restrictions rather than model structure are the main constraint, federated approaches remain a prospective route to cross-site modelling without exchanging raw data, as noted in the section on methodological complexities [103].

Fusion need not begin at the modelling stage. A complementary strategy is to design sampling protocols that capture biological information missing from the sewer signal, addressing at the point of collection the representativeness gaps described in the section on data quality and availability. In long-term care facilities for people with intellectual disabilities, a study protocol has been registered that combines passive sampling of facility sewers with culture of stool obtained from diaper material, in order to estimate the burden of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase- and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales among residents for whom rectal swabbing is considered too burdensome [122]. The protocol illustrates how collection design can be used to address representativeness rather than relying on computational correction alone. Its stated limitations also define what facility-level sampling cannot resolve: wastewater measurements cannot identify individual carriers or distinguish the contributions of residents from those of staff and visitors. Results are not yet available, and the approach remains to be evaluated.

sections.title: Multimodal surveillance beyond centralized sewer networks

paragraphs.en: The same principle extends to settings with partial or absent sewer coverage. The complementary matrices described in the section on real-world implementation can capture signals from populations that are poorly represented or absent from sewer-derived sampling, and passive samplers can integrate signals over time where automated composite sampling is not feasible. Combining these matrices with sewer-derived data creates a multimodal fusion problem in which the streams differ in catchment definition, sampling frequency, and recovery efficiency. Models designed for this setting would need to represent those differences explicitly, through site-level random effects or matrix-specific measurement models, rather than treating all samples as exchangeable observations of a single underlying concentration. Such additional data streams could improve population representativeness and provide more informative inputs for model calibration and public-health interpretation.

sections.title: Mechanistic modelling and uncertainty with digital twins

paragraphs.en: A coupled wastewater digital twin requires an epidemiological and infrastructure model, coherent treatment of uncertainty across the two components, and explicit validation before scenario-based use.

A key future direction is to move beyond purely correlational forecasting toward mechanistic simulation and scenario-based decision support. Digital twins – dynamic digital representations of real-world systems – can in principle integrate wastewater measurements, epidemiological models, mobility patterns, sewer hydraulics, and ML analytics to evaluate how observed wastewater signals relate to underlying infection dynamics. The Catalan digital twin introduced in the section on predictive modelling and forecasting illustrates the epidemiological component of such a coupling: an extended SEIRD simulation of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, continuously validated against the regional sewage surveillance network, in which sewage trends are used to detect discrepancies between simulated and observed dynamics and thereby to reassess the model’s assumptions [11]. The authors are explicit that their aim is not to estimate case numbers from viral loads but to use the wastewater signal as an independent check on a mechanistic model whose clinical inputs had become unreliable as testing policy narrowed. The study reports agreement between simulated and observed trends rather than a formal assessment of predictive uncertainty.

The infrastructure component comes from a different literature. Digital twins for sewer networks and wastewater treatment systems combine real-time sensing, hydraulic models, and data-driven analytics to support simulation, forecasting, and operational control of wastewater infrastructure [84]. Lumley et al. implemented such a twin on the Future City Flow platform for Gothenburg’s regional sewage system, integrating modelling, visualization, forecasting, and model-based predictive control that recommends operational setpoints during storms [83]. Neither of these systems was developed for epidemiological surveillance, and neither has been coupled to a transmission model; they are cited here as the infrastructure layer such a coupling would require rather than as evidence that it has been achieved. They also indicate where uncertainty in that layer originates: the Gothenburg authors identify high-quality online catchment data and, above all, high-quality rainfall forecasts as key requirements, particularly over long prediction horizons [83]. Storm periods are therefore a particularly important source of hydraulic uncertainty.

Coupling the two components raises a question that neither addresses on its own: how uncertainty behaves once they are joined. In a coupled framework, uncertainty propagates along a chain running from sampling and analytical variability, through the estimated concentration, through the hydraulic and in-sewer decay parameters used to convert that concentration into a load, through the inferred number of infections, to the epidemiological state and finally the predicted indicator (Figure 5). These contributions do not simply add. Because load is the product of concentration and flow, uncertainty in these two quantities propagates through a multiplicative step; under the usual small-error and independence approximation, their relative uncertainties combine approximately in quadrature. Uncertainty is therefore likely to be greatest in two operationally important regimes: during storm events, when flow is high and dependent on rainfall forecasts that are themselves uncertain [83], and during low-prevalence periods, when a large proportion of concentration measurements is censored (see the section on data quality and availability). A coupled framework that reports a single uncertainty band without distinguishing these regimes may obscure or understate regime-specific uncertainty.

A second issue is that the two components may quantify different objects. A probabilistic data-driven model may report a predictive interval for a future observation, whereas a mechanistic model may report uncertainty around a latent state or parameter. These intervals are not directly interchangeable because they can represent different sources of uncertainty. Simply propagating one through the other does not guarantee that the nominal interval level will match empirical coverage. Two routes can address this. The first is joint inference, in which the mechanistic structure and the data-driven components are estimated within a single probabilistic model so that a coherent posterior predictive distribution is obtained directly; the semi-mechanistic Bayesian framework discussed in the section on predictive modelling and forecasting illustrates this approach [59]. The second is post hoc verification: whatever the internal construction, the coupled output should be assessed under the established paradigm for probabilistic forecasts, which is to maximize sharpness subject to calibration, using diagnostics such as the probability integral transform histogram, marginal calibration plots, and proper scoring rules [123]. Current reporting practice in wastewater-informed forecasting rarely distinguishes these forms of uncertainty.

Such hybrid frameworks could provide virtual environments for testing surveillance strategies, sampling designs, and resource-allocation scenarios before real-world deployment. Their suitability for scenario testing should be assessed against explicit criteria. Three are particularly relevant. First, a twin intended for strategy testing should reproduce known failure modes of the real system, such as dilution during storm events or the shift in catchment population during holiday periods; a model that reproduces only routine behaviour provides limited evidence about the conditions under which a sampling design would fail. Second, quantities that the twin infers but does not observe, such as the number of infections implied by a measured load, should be checked against an independent source. The longitudinal serological study conducted alongside wastewater surveillance in Alberta long-term care facilities, in which neutralising and anti-nucleocapsid antibody status was measured in residents across four periods of the vaccination programme, illustrates the kind of external reference this requires [78], since internal consistency between the hydraulic and epidemiological components does not establish that an inferred quantity is correct. Third, any scenario comparison should report how its conclusion changes across the plausible range of calibrated parameters; where the ordering of two strategies reverses within that range, the result should be treated as sensitivity-dependent rather than as robust decision support. Applied in this way, digital twins can make the assumptions underlying causal claims explicit and testable, rather than being treated as a direct route to causal inference from wastewater data.
Transparent and actionable ML-enabled WBS requires model explanation, operational decision rules, explicit communication of uncertainty, and deployment designs suited to local capacity.

Future adoption of ML-enabled WBS will require analytics that are transparent and interpretable and outputs that are operationally actionable within ethically governed surveillance systems. One technical response to model opacity is to pair predictive models with explainable-AI (XAI) methods and present the resulting explanations alongside numerical predictions. These methods can help identify which inputs most influence a model’s prediction, but they do not establish whether the prediction is correct or quantify its uncertainty. The SHAP analysis discussed in the section on predictive modelling and forecasting provides the only WBS-specific demonstration identified here, in which feature attribution showed that catchment population and the N gene indicator were the most influential features in an extreme-gradient-boosting model of case counts [55]. Outside this field, a review of 27 studies on explaining machine-learning models for digital health data concluded that explanation methods require further development and validation before they can be relied upon in precision healthcare [85]; the same caution applies to wastewater analytics, where the evidence base is considerably thinner. Model explanations should therefore complement, rather than replace, validation and uncertainty assessment.

Model outputs must also be translated into tools that support rapid decisions, such as thresholds, alerts, uncertainty displays, and dashboards (see the section on real-world implementation). Four operational functions are particularly relevant.

Dynamic thresholding. Static thresholds are vulnerable to environmental change, site-specific variation, and seasonal fluctuation: a concentration associated with surge conditions in one catchment or season may be unremarkable in another, so a fixed cut-off can generate both false alarms and missed signals. Data-derived or site-specific thresholds provide one alternative. In the study discussed in the section on anomaly and fluctuation detection, a clustering model using wastewater, mobility, and clinical data distinguished surge weeks from inter-surge periods with 87.9% accuracy [50]. This demonstrates data-driven risk stratification, but not prospective deployment of an adaptive alert threshold. A clinically anchored threshold requires an outcome series against which the cut-off can be calibrated. Where such data are unavailable, site-specific historical distributions can provide anomaly thresholds, although their public-health meaning still requires validation.

Early-warning alerts. Supervised time-series models can forecast a wastewater-derived or epidemiological indicator and support an alert when the forecast crosses a pre-specified risk boundary. Long short-term memory networks (L3) have been applied to multi-community outbreak prediction in WBS [52]; we identified no WBS evaluation of gated recurrent units for this purpose. The operational value of such alerts depends on lead time and false-alarm rate, not on point accuracy alone, and these metrics should be reported at a stated forecast horizon (see the section on methodological complexities).

Communication of uncertainty. Dashboards can present prediction intervals rather than point estimates alone. One general method is quantile regression forests, which estimate conditional quantiles directly from a fitted ensemble [124]. Because the resulting interval width can vary with the covariates, this approach offers a way to represent predictive uncertainty that changes with the modelled conditions. This flexibility may be useful in WBS, where predictive uncertainty can vary across low-prevalence and storm conditions (see the sections on data quality and availability and on mechanistic modelling and digital twins). The interval's coverage must be verified against observation, and where intervals from data-driven and mechanistic components are displayed together, their differing meaning must be stated (see the section on mechanistic modelling and digital twins).

Deployment under resource constraints. Under resource constraints, simpler models may be preferable when they meet the required operational objective. This matters where computational capacity, technical staff, and network connectivity are limited (see the section on real-world implementation). Local or edge deployment may reduce dependence on continuous network connectivity and external cloud services and can help keep surveillance data within the jurisdiction in which they are generated. As argued in the section on anomaly and fluctuation detection, a more complex model should be adopted only when it improves a pre-specified operational metric against both a naive baseline and the best available simpler alternative.

Beyond technical transparency, ML-enabled WBS will require proactive governance frameworks that define permissible data uses, assign accountability, prevent function creep, and ensure that wastewater-derived intelligence is managed responsibly as surveillance systems scale (see the section on real-world implementation). Operational deployment remains prospective: in the evidence identified in this review, none of these four ML-enabled functions has been prospectively evaluated as part of a routine surveillance programme. Multi-setting validation is therefore needed before they are relied upon for public-health action.

The scope of ML-enabled WBS is extending beyond pathogen monitoring into broader population-health surveillance, notably substance use and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). These applications pose different analytical problems: substance-use surveillance requires harmonization and spatiotemporal integration across analytes and locations, whereas AMR surveillance generates high-dimensional molecular data requiring sequence annotation and interpretation.

Substance-use monitoring is one of the most established non-infectious applications of WBE. Laboratories quantify drug residues and human metabolites in municipal wastewater, aggregate the signals by catchment and sampling period, and infer city-level temporal and geographical patterns of use. A 2023 survey coordinated by SCORE and the European Union Drugs Agency found an established European research and stakeholder infrastructure, with two-thirds of participating countries already using wastewater data to inform drug policy [71]. The same survey identified limitations in generating national estimates from a limited number of sampled cities, sampling frequency for policy use in some countries, and cross-indicator analysis [71]. These limitations echo the problems of representativeness, temporal resolution, and data integration discussed in the section on challenges.

AMR surveillance generates complex population-level molecular data of a different kind. A national programme sampling 47 treatment plants across Wales compared high-throughput qPCR against 73 resistance genes with metagenomic sequencing, and found the two approaches complementary: metagenomics detected 545 genes and provided the bacterial host context needed for risk assessment, whereas HT-qPCR quantified all targeted genes including clinically relevant ones present at low abundance, and both recovered the same spatiotemporal separation between hospital and municipal resistomes [67]. At the analytical level, deep-learning-based ARG annotation provides a relevant methodological tool, although the evidence cited here comes from bioinformatics rather than from an ML model deployed in WBS [68]. ML could contribute to AMR surveillance through sequence annotation, spatial pattern analysis, and interpretation of high-dimensional resistome profiles using approaches such as those reviewed in the section on visualization and interpretation of high-dimensional data.

sections.title: Endogenous biomarkers and broader health signals

paragraphs.en: Wastewater can also capture endogenous biomarkers beyond infectious and resistance-related targets. Endogenous stress hormones have been quantified in wastewater from a university campus of approximately 26,000 people, with reproducible weekly cycles in cortisol and cortisone excretion, significantly higher levels on weekdays than at weekends, and elevated levels during the first two months of each semester [70]; expert commentary describes wastewater as carrying endogenous and exogenous metabolites reflecting lifestyle, diet, exposure, and health status alongside pathogens [125]. These sources establish the feasibility of measuring broader population-level biomarkers, not the performance of ML models using them. Combining such biomarkers with chemical, environmental, and contextual measurements could nevertheless create multimodal datasets for future ML analysis.

Technical feasibility does not by itself establish that an application is acceptable or appropriate for surveillance. The public survey discussed in the section on real-world implementation found support for wastewater surveillance of disease at 91% but of lifestyle behaviours at 35%, of healthy eating at 37%, and of mental illness at 46%, and found support declining as the geographic scale became smaller and less anonymous [117]. These findings show that acceptability depends on both the surveillance target and spatial resolution. Expansion toward behavioural or lifestyle monitoring should therefore be preceded by explicit governance and community-engagement frameworks rather than introduced solely because the measurements are technically possible.

Together, these examples broaden the potential scope of ML-enabled WBS beyond pathogen trend monitoring, but the maturity of the evidence differs substantially among applications. Substance-use WBE is operationally established, AMR produces data well suited to high-dimensional analysis but has limited demonstrated ML deployment, and endogenous-biomarker studies establish measurement feasibility rather than ML-enabled decision support. Broader population-health surveillance should therefore develop in step with both analytical evidence and public acceptability.

sections.title: Analytical framework and strength of evidence

paragraphs.en: Wastewater-based surveillance has become an important population-level tool for monitoring infectious disease dynamics, but wastewater measurements are not directly equivalent to public-health indicators. Their interpretation requires analytical workflows that can distinguish true epidemiological signals from technical, environmental, and population-related noise. This review organized the analytical methods used in WBS into four layers – classical statistical models, conventional machine learning, deep learning, and hybrid or mechanistically informed approaches – and applied that classification consistently across applications, challenges, and future directions. Classical statistical models remain central to trend description, correlation and lag–lead analysis, signal processing, and early-warning interpretation, and account for most of the demonstrated results reviewed here; machine learning adds capacity for heterogeneous, high-dimensional, nonlinear, and multimodal data, and demonstrated gains from ML have been concentrated mainly in multivariable settings where clinical and contextual covariates are available.

Current ML applications in WBS span predictive modelling and forecasting, anomaly and fluctuation detection, data harmonization and normalization, high-dimensional interpretation, and integrated decision support. The strength of the evidence supporting them is markedly uneven (Table 2). Quantitative modelling evidence is strongly concentrated in SARS-CoV-2, for which hospitalization and case forecasting, outbreak-risk classification, and trend-deviation detection have all been reported. For influenza viruses and respiratory syncytial virus, published work remains correlational or descriptive; for enteric and hepatitis viruses, mpox virus, poliovirus, bacterial and protozoan pathogens, and antimicrobial resistance determinants, machine-learning applications are at present prospective rather than demonstrated. Conclusions about the predictive and early-warning performance of ML in WBS should therefore be interpreted primarily in the context of SARS-CoV-2 surveillance under unusually favourable data conditions, and generalization to other pathogens remains an open question. Even within SARS-CoV-2 surveillance, reported performance is strongly context-dependent: forecast accuracy depends strongly on sampling frequency and training-set size [58], and adding wastewater data improved or degraded forecasts substantially at particular locations and dates while leaving overall performance essentially unchanged [59].

Practical reliability is constrained by a further set of factors that operate upstream of any model: data incompleteness and censoring, sampling variability, inconsistent laboratory and reporting practices, limited external validation under time- and space-aware designs, model opacity, operational cost, and governance requirements. These constraints affect model families differently. Many L1 methods can be fitted to the wastewater series itself, whereas supervised L2 and L3 models generally require paired outcomes and larger training sets; L4 approaches additionally require mechanistic or system-level information. Computational and maintenance demands also vary with model complexity and deployment context. Greater model complexity should therefore be justified by improvement in a pre-specified operational metric against both a naive baseline and the best available simpler alternative. ML is most appropriately used as decision support within broader public-health surveillance and expert interpretation, rather than as an autonomous decision system.

Future WBS systems may develop from pathogen-specific monitoring platforms into integrated population-health intelligence systems supporting outbreak preparedness, pandemic response, and One Health surveillance. Realizing this will require closing the gaps identified in Table 2, in particular the scarcity of validated ML models for targets other than SARS-CoV-2 and for settings not served by centralized sewer networks. Progress will depend on standardized collaborative frameworks, harmonized data infrastructures, multimodal data fusion, mechanistic and digital-twin modelling with explicit uncertainty assessment, transparent and explainable analytics, and governance mechanisms that define responsible data use and accountability. The scope of ML-enabled WBS could also extend beyond pathogen monitoring toward antimicrobial resistance, substance use, and other population-health biomarkers. Public acceptability is substantially lower for behavioural and lifestyle targets and at smaller geographic scales (see the section on real-world implementation), so such expansion will need to reflect public acceptability as well as analytical feasibility. Under these conditions, ML can help move WBS from retrospective signal reporting toward proactive, interpretable, and scalable public-health surveillance.

figures.label: Figure 1.
figures.caption: Workflow of machine learning-enabled wastewater surveillance. The framework comprises six interconnected stages (1) sampling of wastewater from diverse sources using appropriate strategies; (2) laboratory analysis including sample processing and pathogen detection; (3) data management and harmonization of multi-source heterogeneous data; (4) machine learning analytics for predictive modelling, anomaly detection, and pattern discovery; (5) generation of outputs, visualization, and communication; and (6) translation of insights into public health actions. Abbreviations: qPCR, quantitative polymerase chain reaction; dPCR, digital PCR; ELISA, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; AMR, antimicrobial resistance; ML, machine learning.

figures.label: Figure 2.
figures.caption: Multimodal data integration and translation to public-health decision support in machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance (WBS). Multiple wastewater, epidemiological, clinical, environmental, sewer-system, population, and contextual data streams are integrated and harmonized before analysis using statistical and machine-learning approaches. Analytical outputs are transformed into surveillance indicators, including early-warning alerts, trend estimates, forecasting results, and variant/AMR profiles, which support public-health interpretation, risk assessment, resource allocation, targeted interventions, and policy decision-making. Continuous feedback enables data reprocessing and model updating.

figures.label: Figure 3.
figures.caption: Challenges and future directions of machine learning in wastewater-based surveillance (WBS). Major challenges for machine learning-enabled WBS include limitations in data quality and availability, methodological complexities in model development and interpretation, and barriers to real-world implementation, scalability, and governance. Future directions focus on standardized data frameworks, multimodal data integration, digital-twin-based mechanistic modelling, explainable and trustworthy analytics, and expansion of WBS applications beyond pathogen surveillance to broader population-health monitoring. Arrows indicate the interrelationships between current challenges and potential future solutions.

figures.label: Figure 4.
figures.caption: Assumed causal structure underlying multimodal wastewater-based surveillance modelling. Community infection prevalence is not directly observed but causes both the measured wastewater signal and reported cases; the association that a predictive model actually fits (thick arrow) is therefore not itself causal. Environmental and seasonal variables, represented here as potential confounders, may act as common causes of both endpoints of that association: rainfall can affect the wastewater signal through dilution and changes in flow while also influencing human movement and transmission, while season and temperature can additionally affect in-sewer decay and pathogen circulation. Such variables may therefore open backdoor paths that should be addressed when the analytical objective is causal, but they may legitimately remain in a predictive model when the objective is prediction alone. The dash-dotted arrow denotes surveillance bias: testing intensity affects reported cases without affecting shedding, so a model trained against reported cases may partly learn features of surveillance behaviour rather than of transmission. This graph is illustrative; the appropriate structure is pathogen- and setting-specific and should be stated explicitly for each analysis.

figures.label: Figure 5.
figures.caption: Growth of uncertainty along a coupled wastewater digital-twin chain. The horizontal line represents the true value at each stage of the chain, and the envelope around it represents the uncertainty attached to that estimate; its vertical extent at any point is the magnitude of uncertainty at that stage. Each stage introduces further uncertainty, which is carried forward into all subsequent stages, so the envelope widens from left to right. The widening is gradual across the additive steps but may become particularly pronounced at the conversion of concentration into load, because load is the product of concentration and flow and, under a small-error and independence approximation, the relative uncertainties of the two factors combine approximately in quadrature rather than adding directly. This expansion may be particularly large during storm events, when flow is high and poorly constrained, and during low-prevalence periods, when a large proportion of concentration measurements is censored.
